translations.note: Burton joins two sources here. The first three lines are adapted from Terence, Eunuchus 59–61 ('In amore haec omnia insunt vitia: iniuriae, suspiciones, inimicitiae, indutiae, bellum, pax rursum'). Burton's 'audaciae' ('acts of daring') stands where Terence has other words. The rest comes from Plautus, Mercator, in the opening speech of the play. Plautus reads 'incogitantia' ('thoughtlessness'), while Burton has 'excogitantia', which would mean 'contriving'. Burton's own English 'devices' follows his reading, so the translation does too. 'Aviditias' is a misprint for 'aviditas' ('greed').

burton_span.exact: Dost ask (my dear) what service I will have? / To love me day and night is all I crave, / To dream on me, to expect, to think on me, / Depend and hope, still covet me to see, / Delight thyself in me, be wholly mine, / For know my love, that I am wholly thine.

source.basis: Phaedria's well-known reply to Thais ('egone quid velim? dies noctesque me ames...'); Burton's sidenote in the preceding paragraph reads "Ter. Eunuch. Act. 1 sc. 2."

3.2.3.1-f99.text: ——— egone quid velim? / Dies noctesque ames me, me desideres, / Me somnies, me expectes, me cogites, / Me speres, me te oblectes, mecum tota sis, / Meus fac postremo animus, quando ego sum tuus.

translations.note: Burton's text differs a little from the standard Terence: it has 'ames me' for 'me ames', 'me cogites' for 'de me cogites', and drops 'sis' from 'meus fac sis postremo animus'. The sense is the same.
